title: Multiplying and Dividing by One-Digit Numbers
seo_title: Grade 4 Multiplying and Dividing by One-Digit Numbers Worksheets: Area Models, Remainders (Free, BC Curriculum)
short_title: Multiplying and dividing by one-digit numbers
standard_text: Multiplication and division of two- or three-digit numbers by one-digit numbers
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 math worksheets on multiplying and dividing by one-digit numbers for the BC curriculum: base ten blocks, area models, partial products, the standard method, sharing with trading, remainders and BC word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, great FSA practice.
key_big: Split the number into hundreds, tens and ones. Multiply or share each part, then put the parts together.
key_sub: 23 × 4 = 20 × 4 + 3 × 4 = 80 + 12 = 92. To divide, share the biggest blocks first and trade what is left. A remainder is always less than the divisor; in a word problem, decide if you need one more.
body_html:
Multiply: split the number into tens and ones

23 × 4 means 4 groups of 23. Each 23 is 2 tens and 3 ones. Multiply the tens, multiply the ones, then add.

An area model shows the same thing. The rectangle is 23 long and 4 wide. Split 23 into 20 and 3.

Partial products and the standard method

Partial products write each part on its own row, then add the rows. The standard method is a short way to write the same steps. Start with the ones. If you get 10 or more, write the ones digit and regroup the tens: write a small digit above the next place. Multiply first, then add the regrouped digit.

Three digits

236 × 4 = ?

Ones: 6 × 4 = 24. Write 4, regroup 2 tens. Tens: 3 × 4 = 12, plus 2 = 14. Write 4, regroup 1 hundred. Hundreds: 2 × 4 = 8, plus 1 = 9.

Answer: 944

Check with an estimate: 236 is close to 200, and 200 × 4 = 800. 944 is a bit more, so it makes sense.

Divide by sharing

52 ÷ 4 means share 52 into 4 equal groups. Share the biggest blocks first. When some are left, trade them for 10 of the next smaller block and keep sharing.

You can also split the number into parts that divide easily. 156 ÷ 4: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 and 36 ÷ 4 = 9, so 156 ÷ 4 = 39. Check by multiplying: 39 × 4 = 156.

Remainders

Sometimes there is some left that cannot make another full group. That is the remainder. We write it with R. The remainder is always less than the number you divide by.

What does the remainder mean?

The question asksUse the remainder like this75 people, 9 in each shuttle bus: 75 ÷ 9 = 8 R 3
How many are needed for everyone?Add 1 to the answer9 buses
How many full groups?Leave the remainder out8 full buses
How many are left over?The remainder is the answer3 people

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Forgetting to regroup (23 × 4 = 82)12 ones = 1 ten and 2 ones. Add the 1 ten to the tens: 92
Multiplying only the ones (23 × 4 = 32)Multiply the tens too: 20 × 4 = 80, 3 × 4 = 12, 80 + 12 = 92
Writing 20 × 4 as 820 × 4 = 2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80
Ignoring the remainder (75 people need 8 buses)3 people are still waiting, so 9 buses are needed
A remainder that is too big (38 ÷ 5 = 6 R 8)If the remainder is 5 or more, make one more group: 7 R 3

faq.q: How do Grade 4 students in BC multiply and divide by one-digit numbers?
faq.a: The BC curriculum asks Grade 4 students to multiply and divide two- and three-digit numbers by one-digit numbers using strategies that make sense, such as base ten blocks, area models and partial products. Many students then move on to a shorter written method.

faq.q: What is the area model for multiplication?
faq.a: It is a rectangle split into parts by place value. For 23 × 4, one part is 20 × 4 = 80 and the other is 3 × 4 = 12, and the whole rectangle is 80 + 12 = 92.

faq.q: What does R mean in a division answer?
faq.a: R stands for remainder, the amount left over after making equal groups. In a word problem, decide what it means: sometimes you need one more bus or box, and sometimes you leave the leftovers out.

faq.q: Is multiplication and division on the Grade 4 FSA?
faq.a: The Grade 4 FSA numeracy section asks students to solve problems with numbers, so multiplying, dividing and explaining what a remainder means are useful practice. These worksheets give that practice with an answer key.

items.e: Ones: 2 × 9 = 18. Write 8, regroup 1 ten. Tens: 0 × 9 = 0, plus 1 = 1. Write 1. Hundreds: 9 × 9 = 81. Write 81. Answer: 8118. 0 × 9 = 0, but you still add the regrouped 1.

sets.title: Divide by sharing and with base ten

items.e: Share 6 tens: each group gets 2 tens. Share 9 ones: each group gets 3 ones. Each group gets 23. Check: 23 × 3 = 69.

1 hundred is not enough for 4 groups. Trade it for 10 tens. Now there are 13 tens. Share 13 tens: each group gets 3 tens, 1 ten left. Trade it for 10 ones. Now there are 12 ones. Share 12 ones: each group gets 3 ones. Each group gets 33. Check: 33 × 4 = 132.
Share 2 hundreds: each group gets 1 hundred. Share 4 tens: each group gets 2 tens. Share 6 ones: each group gets 3 ones. Each group gets 123. Check: 123 × 2 = 246.

items.q: What is 138 ÷ 3?
items.e: 1 hundred is not enough for 3 groups. Trade it for 10 tens. Now there are 13 tens. Share 13 tens: each group gets 4 tens, 1 ten left. Trade it for 10 ones. Now there are 18 ones. Share 18 ones: each group gets 6 ones. Each group gets 46. Check: 46 × 3 = 138.
Share 7 tens: each group gets 2 tens, 1 ten left. Trade it for 10 ones. Now there are 12 ones. Share 12 ones: each group gets 4 ones. Each group gets 24. Check: 24 × 3 = 72.

items.q: What is 256 ÷ 8?

items.q: What is 91 ÷ 7?
items.e: Share 9 tens: each group gets 1 ten, 2 tens left. Trade them for 20 ones. Now there are 21 ones. Share 21 ones: each group gets 3 ones. Each group gets 13. Check: 13 × 7 = 91.

items.q: Use the area model to find 378 ÷ 6.

items.q: What is 84 ÷ 6?

items.q: You share 1 hundred, 3 tens and 2 ones equally into 4 groups. There are not enough hundreds. What do you do first?

Share 4 tens: each group gets 1 ten. Share 8 ones: each group gets 2 ones. Each group gets 12. Check: 12 × 4 = 48.

items.q: To find 75 ÷ 5, you share 7 tens: each group gets 1 ten and 2 tens are left. You trade the 2 tens for ones. How many ones are there to share now?
items.e: 2 tens = 20 ones. Add the 5 ones you already had: 20 + 5 = 25 ones. 25 ÷ 5 = 5, so 75 ÷ 5 = 15.

items.q: You share 5 tens equally into 4 groups. Each group gets 1 ten. What do you do with the 1 ten that is left?
items.e: Every group must get the same amount, so do not leave it out or give it to one group. Trade 1 ten for 10 ones and keep sharing. For 52 ÷ 4: 10 + 2 = 12 ones, so each group gets 3 more ones. 52 ÷ 4 = 13.

items.q: What number goes in the box? ☐ × 8 = 96
items.e: Think: 8 times what number is 96? That is 96 ÷ 8. Share 9 tens: each group gets 1 ten, 1 ten left. Trade it for 10 ones. Now there are 16 ones. Share 16 ones: each group gets 2 ones. Each group gets 12. Check: 12 × 8 = 96.

sets.title: Division with remainders and what the remainder means

items.q: Olivia says 77 ÷ 6 = 11 R 11. What mistake did she make?
items.e: The remainder must be less than the divisor. 11 is more than 6, so one more group of 6 fits: 11 − 6 = 5. The answer is 12 R 5. Check: 12 × 6 + 5 = 77.

items.q: The picture shows 31 counters in groups of 3. What is 31 ÷ 3?
items.e: Make groups of 3. There are 10 full groups and 1 counter left over (in red). 1 is less than 3, so it cannot make another group. 31 ÷ 3 = 10 R 1. Check: 10 × 3 + 1 = 31.

items.q: The picture shows 27 counters in groups of 4. What is 27 ÷ 4?
items.e: Make groups of 4. There are 6 full groups and 3 counters left over (in red). 3 is less than 4, so it cannot make another group. 27 ÷ 4 = 6 R 3. Check: 6 × 4 + 3 = 27.

items.q: What is 98 ÷ 4?
items.e: Share 9 tens: each group gets 2 tens, 1 ten left. Trade it for 10 ones. Now there are 18 ones. Share 18 ones: each group gets 4 ones, 2 ones left over. Each group gets 24 and 2 are left over: 24 R 2. Check: 24 × 4 + 2 = 98.
Make groups of 5. There are 7 full groups and 3 counters left over (in red). 3 is less than 5, so it cannot make another group. 38 ÷ 5 = 7 R 3. Check: 7 × 5 + 3 = 38.

items.q: What is 56 ÷ 3?
items.e: Share 5 tens: each group gets 1 ten, 2 tens left. Trade them for 20 ones. Now there are 26 ones. Share 26 ones: each group gets 8 ones, 2 ones left over. Each group gets 18 and 2 are left over: 18 R 2. Check: 18 × 3 + 2 = 56.

items.q: 948 ÷ 5 = 189 R 3. Which expression checks this answer? It should equal 948.
items.e: Multiply the quotient by the divisor, then add the remainder: 189 × 5 = 945, 945 + 3 = 948. It matches, so the answer is right.

items.q: Zara says 83 ÷ 6 = 12 R 11. What mistake did she make?
items.e: The remainder must be less than the divisor. 11 is more than 6, so one more group of 6 fits: 11 − 6 = 5. The answer is 13 R 5. Check: 13 × 6 + 5 = 83.
Make groups of 6. There are 7 full groups and 2 counters left over (in red). 2 is less than 6, so it cannot make another group. 44 ÷ 6 = 7 R 2. Check: 7 × 6 + 2 = 44.

items.q: You divide a number by 4. Which of these could be the remainder?
items.e: A remainder is always less than the divisor. When you divide by 4, the remainder can only be 0 to 3. So 3 is the only possible one.

items.q: What is the remainder when 842 is divided by 9?
items.e: The question asks for the remainder, not the quotient. 8 hundreds are not enough for 9 groups. Trade them for 80 tens. Now there are 84 tens. Share 84 tens: each group gets 9 tens, 3 tens left. Trade them for 30 ones. Now there are 32 ones. Share 32 ones: each group gets 3 ones, 5 ones left over. Each group gets 93 and 5 are left over: 93 R 5. Check: 93 × 9 + 5 = 842.

items.q: What is the remainder when 551 is divided by 7?
items.e: The question asks for the remainder, not the quotient. 5 hundreds are not enough for 7 groups. Trade them for 50 tens. Now there are 55 tens. Share 55 tens: each group gets 7 tens, 6 tens left. Trade them for 60 ones. Now there are 61 ones. Share 61 ones: each group gets 8 ones, 5 ones left over. Each group gets 78 and 5 are left over: 78 R 5. Check: 78 × 7 + 5 = 551.

items.q: 266 ÷ 9 = 29 R 5. Which expression checks this answer? It should equal 266.
items.e: Multiply the quotient by the divisor, then add the remainder: 29 × 9 = 261, 261 + 5 = 266. It matches, so the answer is right.

items.q: What is 686 ÷ 8?
items.e: 6 hundreds are not enough for 8 groups. Trade them for 60 tens. Now there are 68 tens. Share 68 tens: each group gets 8 tens, 4 tens left. Trade them for 40 ones. Now there are 46 ones. Share 46 ones: each group gets 5 ones, 6 ones left over. Each group gets 85 and 6 are left over: 85 R 6. Check: 85 × 8 + 6 = 686.

items.q: What is 779 ÷ 4?
items.e: Share 7 hundreds: each group gets 1 hundred, 3 hundreds left. Trade them for 30 tens. Now there are 37 tens. Share 37 tens: each group gets 9 tens, 1 ten left. Trade it for 10 ones. Now there are 19 ones. Share 19 ones: each group gets 4 ones, 3 ones left over. Each group gets 194 and 3 are left over: 194 R 3. Check: 194 × 4 + 3 = 779.

items.q: 27 ÷ 4 = 6 R 3. There are 27 cookies and 4 cookies go in each bag. What does the 3 mean?
items.e: 6 bags are full (6 × 4 = 24 cookies). 27 − 24 = 3 cookies do not fill another bag. The remainder 3 is the cookies left over.

items.q: What is 392 ÷ 6?
items.e: 3 hundreds are not enough for 6 groups. Trade them for 30 tens. Now there are 39 tens. Share 39 tens: each group gets 6 tens, 3 tens left. Trade them for 30 ones. Now there are 32 ones. Share 32 ones: each group gets 5 ones, 2 ones left over. Each group gets 65 and 2 are left over: 65 R 2. Check: 65 × 6 + 2 = 392.

items.q: You divide a number by 6. Which of these could be the remainder?
items.e: A remainder is always less than the divisor. When you divide by 6, the remainder can only be 0 to 5. So 5 is the only possible one.

items.q: 50 ÷ 8 = 6 R 2. There are 50 students and 8 students fit in each van. What does the 2 mean?
items.e: 6 vans carry 6 × 8 = 48 students. 50 − 48 = 2 students are still waiting, so they need a 7th van.

items.q: What is 93 ÷ 6?
items.e: Share 9 tens: each group gets 1 ten, 3 tens left. Trade them for 30 ones. Now there are 33 ones. Share 33 ones: each group gets 5 ones, 3 ones left over. Each group gets 15 and 3 are left over: 15 R 3. Check: 15 × 6 + 3 = 93.

sets.title: Word problems: buses, apples and more

items.q: A box of Okanagan apples holds 88 apples. A fruit stand in Kelowna sells 6 boxes. How many apples is that?
items.e: Equal groups, so multiply: 88 apples × 6. Ones: 8 × 6 = 48. Write 8, regroup 4 tens. Tens: 8 × 6 = 48, plus 4 = 52. Write 52. Answer: 528. So the answer is 528 apples.

items.q: Arjun buys 6 swim passes at $14 each. He pays with $100. How much change does he get?
items.e: Step 1: cost: 6 × $14 = $84 (4 × 6 = 24, write 4, regroup 2; 1 × 6 = 6, plus 2 = 8). Step 2: change: $100 − $84 = $16.

items.q: A farm stand in Penticton has 230 peaches. It packs them in boxes of 4 and fills as many boxes as it can. How many peaches are not in a box?
items.e: Divide: 230 ÷ 4 = 57 R 2 (57 × 4 = 228, 230 − 228 = 2). The question asks how many are left over. That is the remainder: 2 peaches.

items.q: Wei reads a 168-page book in 7 days. He reads the same number of pages each day. How many pages does he read each day?
items.e: Share equally, so divide: 168 ÷ 7. 1 hundred is not enough for 7 groups. Trade it for 10 tens. Now there are 16 tens. Share 16 tens: each group gets 2 tens, 2 tens left. Trade them for 20 ones. Now there are 28 ones. Share 28 ones: each group gets 4 ones. Each group gets 24. Check: 24 × 7 = 168. So the answer is 24 pages.

items.q: A class of 29 students goes to a soccer game. Each van holds 6 students. How many vans are needed?
items.e: Divide: 29 ÷ 6 = 4 R 5 (4 × 6 = 24, 29 − 24 = 5). 4 vans hold only 24. The 5 students left over still need a seat, so add 1 more. The answer is 5 vans.

items.q: 52 campers go canoeing on a lake near Kamloops. Each canoe holds 3 campers. How many canoes do they need?
items.e: Divide: 52 ÷ 3 = 17 R 1 (17 × 3 = 51, 52 − 51 = 1). 17 canoes hold only 51. The 1 camper left over still needs a canoe, so add 1 more. The answer is 18 canoes.

items.q: 75 students and adults go on a field trip to the aquarium. Each shuttle bus holds 9 people. How many shuttle buses are needed to take everyone?
items.e: Divide: 75 ÷ 9 = 8 R 3 (8 × 9 = 72, 75 − 72 = 3). 8 buses hold only 72. The 3 people left over still need a seat, so add 1 more. The answer is 9 buses.

items.q: Tickets to a hockey game cost $27 each. Simran buys 5 tickets for her family. How much does she pay?
items.e: Equal groups, so multiply: $27 × 5. Ones: 7 × 5 = 35. Write 5, regroup 3 tens. Tens: 2 × 5 = 10, plus 3 = 13. Write 13. Answer: 135. So the answer is $135.

items.q: A small ferry to an island carries 48 cars on each trip. It makes 7 trips in a day. How many cars is that?
items.e: Equal groups, so multiply: 48 cars × 7. Ones: 8 × 7 = 56. Write 6, regroup 5 tens. Tens: 4 × 7 = 28, plus 5 = 33. Write 33. Answer: 336. So the answer is 336 cars.

items.q: A trail loop in Stanley Park is 875 m long. Jasleen walks the loop 4 times. How far does she walk?
items.e: Equal groups, so multiply: 875 m × 4. Ones: 5 × 4 = 20. Write 0, regroup 2 tens. Tens: 7 × 4 = 28, plus 2 = 30. Write 0, regroup 3 hundreds. Hundreds: 8 × 4 = 32, plus 3 = 35. Write 35. Answer: 3500. So the answer is 3500 m.

items.q: 96 students come to a soccer day in Burnaby. They make 4 equal teams. How many students are on each team?
items.e: Share equally, so divide: 96 ÷ 4. Share 9 tens: each group gets 2 tens, 1 ten left. Trade it for 10 ones. Now there are 16 ones. Share 16 ones: each group gets 4 ones. Each group gets 24. Check: 24 × 4 = 96. So the answer is 24 students.

items.q: A Grade 4 class reads for 25 minutes every school day. How many minutes is that in 9 school days?
items.e: Equal groups, so multiply: 25 minutes × 9. Ones: 5 × 9 = 45. Write 5, regroup 4 tens. Tens: 2 × 9 = 18, plus 4 = 22. Write 22. Answer: 225. So the answer is 225 minutes.

items.q: A school books 4 small buses for a trip to Whistler. Each bus has 36 seats. 129 people go on the trip. How many seats are empty?
items.e: Step 1: seats: 4 × 36 = 144 (6 × 4 = 24, write 4, regroup 2; 3 × 4 = 12, plus 2 = 14). Step 2: empty seats: 144 − 129 = 15.

items.q: An orchard in the Okanagan picked 467 apples. It packs them in gift boxes of 8. How many boxes can it fill completely?
items.e: Divide: 467 ÷ 8 = 58 R 3 (58 × 8 = 464, 467 − 464 = 3). The 3 apples left over are not enough to fill another box, so leave the remainder out. The answer is 58 boxes.

items.q: A cedar board is 192 cm long. It is cut into 8 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
items.e: Share equally, so divide: 192 ÷ 8. 1 hundred is not enough for 8 groups. Trade it for 10 tens. Now there are 19 tens. Share 19 tens: each group gets 2 tens, 3 tens left. Trade them for 30 ones. Now there are 32 ones. Share 32 ones: each group gets 4 ones. Each group gets 24. Check: 24 × 8 = 192. So the answer is 24 cm.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, each of 8 classes at a Surrey school raises $135. How much do they raise in all?
items.e: Equal groups, so multiply: $135 × 8. Ones: 5 × 8 = 40. Write 0, regroup 4 tens. Tens: 3 × 8 = 24, plus 4 = 28. Write 8, regroup 2 hundreds. Hundreds: 1 × 8 = 8, plus 2 = 10. Write 10. Answer: 1080. So the answer is $1080.

items.q: Ethan has $40. A swim pass costs $6. How many swim passes can he buy?
items.e: Divide: 40 ÷ 6 = 6 R 4 (6 × 6 = 36, 40 − 36 = 4). The $4 left over is not enough to buy another pass, so leave the remainder out. The answer is 6 passes.

items.q: 118 students go on an overnight trip on Vancouver Island. Each tent sleeps 4 students. How many tents are needed?
items.e: Divide: 118 ÷ 4 = 29 R 2 (29 × 4 = 116, 118 − 116 = 2). 29 tents hold only 116. The 2 students left over still need a tent, so add 1 more. The answer is 30 tents.

items.q: A salmon hatchery has 6 tanks. Each tank holds 245 young salmon. How many young salmon are there?
items.e: Equal groups, so multiply: 245 salmon × 6. Ones: 5 × 6 = 30. Write 0, regroup 3 tens. Tens: 4 × 6 = 24, plus 3 = 27. Write 7, regroup 2 hundreds. Hundreds: 2 × 6 = 12, plus 2 = 14. Write 14. Answer: 1470. So the answer is 1470 salmon.

items.q: A teacher shares 75 pencil crayons equally among 9 tables. Each table gets as many as possible. How many pencil crayons are left over?
items.e: Divide: 75 ÷ 9 = 8 R 3 (8 × 9 = 72, 75 − 72 = 3). The question asks how many are left over. That is the remainder: 3 pencil crayons.
